readings.title: Hymn II (“Come, let us go forth into the fields”)
readings.challenge: Picture each young creature in turn, then notice where the hymn stops describing and starts speaking to them.
readings.focus: A spring walk turns into thanks spoken on behalf of creatures that cannot speak.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” Goslings are baby geese; the lambs’ dams are their mothers; “just dropt” means just born; dumb here means unable to speak.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share. Its claim that people are “better” than animals is the author’s view.

excerpt.locator: Hymn II, the complete hymn; opens “COME, let us go forth into the fields, let us see how the flowers spring, let us listen…”; closes “…green field, we will offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and the incense of praise.”.

questions.prompt: Name four young creatures in the hymn and what each one is doing.
facilitatorNotes: Goslings run on the green, chickens come out of their shells, lambs totter beside their mothers, and butterflies open their wings to the sun.
evidence: The young goslings are running upon the green,
they totter by the side of their dams,

questions.prompt: Why do the old geese hiss? And why does the hymn tell the lambs not to worry if they fall?
facilitatorNotes: The geese protect their just-hatched goslings. The lambs will land on soft grass, which the hymn says was spread “on purpose” for them: even the ground seems to care for them.
evidence: the old ones hiss with anger if any one comes near.
there is spread under you a carpet of soft grass,

questions.prompt: The hymn tells the trees and lambs, “you are dumb, we will say it for you.” What does it promise to say for them?
facilitatorNotes: How good their maker is: the people will give thanks on behalf of creatures that cannot speak.
evidence: you are dumb, we will say it for you.

questions.prompt: The author writes, “we are better than they.” What reason does she give? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Because people can praise God aloud with their tongues. Some readers will agree; others will point out that the hymn itself says the animals are “glad to be alive,” which may be a kind of thanks too. Ask for a line to support each view.
evidence: we are better than they, and can praise him better.
they are glad to be alive,

readings.title: Hymn IV (“Come, and I will shew you what is beautiful”)
readings.challenge: Find a sentence pattern that repeats three times, and say what it is for.
readings.focus: Beauty, strength and glory are each shown in something real, then traced back to their maker.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” “Shew” is an old spelling of “show” and “desart” of “desert”; a lair is a wild animal’s den; a countenance is a face.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share.

excerpt.locator: Hymn IV, the complete hymn; opens “COME, and I will shew you what is beautiful. It is a rose full blown. See how she sits…”; closes “…is beauty; they are strong, but he is strength; they are perfect, but he is perfection.”.

questions.prompt: What three things does the hymn show, and what quality is each one an example of?
facilitatorNotes: A rose in full bloom (beautiful), a lion (strong) and the sun (glorious).
evidence: It is a rose full blown.
I will shew you what is strong.
I will shew you what is glorious.

questions.prompt: How does the hymn make the lion seem strong without telling his size?
facilitatorNotes: It shows what the other animals do when he roars: cattle run and wild beasts hide.
evidence: the cattle of the field fly, and the wild beasts of the desart hide themselves,

questions.prompt: After each example comes the same kind of sentence. What is the pattern?
facilitatorNotes: “The lion is strong, but he that made the lion is stronger than he”: something great, then its maker as greater. The pattern repeats for the rose and the sun, which makes the hymn easy to learn and say together.
evidence: The lion is strong, but he that made the lion is stronger than he:
She is beautiful, but there is a fairer than she.

questions.prompt: The end says, “they are beautiful, but he is beauty.” What is the difference between being beautiful and being beauty?
facilitatorNotes: A rose has beauty as one of its qualities; the author believes God is where beauty itself comes from. It is a hard idea; accept careful explanations and examples.
evidence: they are beautiful, but he is beauty;

readings.title: Hymn V (“The glorious sun is set in the west”)
readings.challenge: Listen for sounds that have stopped, and follow a comparison between a mother and God.
readings.focus: As the world goes quiet for the night, the hymn asks who keeps watch over sleepers.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” Sultry means hot and heavy; woodbine is honeysuckle; a smith hammers hot iron on an anvil; to “still” a noise is to quiet it.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share.

excerpt.locator: Hymn V, the complete hymn; opens “THE glorious sun is set in the west; the night-dews fall; and the air which was sultry,…”; closes “…praise be in our hearts, when we lie down; let his praise be on our lips, when we awake.”.

questions.prompt: List the sounds that have stopped now that night has come.
facilitatorNotes: The bees’ murmur, the sheep’s bleating, voices, children at play, hurrying feet, the smith’s hammer and the carpenter’s saw.
evidence: There is no murmur of bees around the hive,
The smith's hammer is not heard upon the anvil;

questions.prompt: Why does the hymn ask who takes care of people while they sleep?
facilitatorNotes: Sleepers cannot defend themselves or see danger coming. The question makes the reader feel how helpless sleep is before the answer comes.
evidence: when they cannot defend themselves, nor see if danger approacheth?

questions.prompt: The hymn compares God with a mother. What does the mother do, and what does God do that is like it?
facilitatorNotes: She moves quietly with her finger on her lips and draws the bed curtains; God draws “the curtains of darkness” and hushes everything so “his large family” can sleep. Night itself becomes a kind of care.
evidence: As the mother moveth about the house with her finger on her lips,
so God draweth the curtains of darkness around us;

questions.prompt: At the end the hymn speaks to flowers and birds. What does it ask them to do, and why might it end with morning?
facilitatorNotes: Flowers should open and smell sweet, and birds should sing their thanks before they sing to their mates. Ending with waking completes a whole night, from sunset to sunrise, and turns rest into a reason for thanks.
evidence: Flowers, when you open again, spread your leaves,
sing to him, before you sing to your mates.

readings.title: Hymn VI (“Child of reason, whence comest thou?”)
readings.challenge: Read a hymn written for two voices, and track how the questions repeat.
readings.focus: A child reports what was seen and heard; a second voice asks what was missed.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” Barbauld wrote some hymns “in alternate parts,” for two voices; this one can be read by two people. “Whence comest thou?” means “Where have you come from?” The firmament is the sky; a harebell is a small blue wildflower.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share.

excerpt.locator: Hymn VI, the complete hymn; opens “CHILD of reason, whence comest thou? What has thine eye observed, and whither has thy…”; closes “…nothing, O child of reason, is without God;–let God therefore be in all thy thoughts.”.

questions.prompt: Who asks the questions in this hymn, and who answers? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: A voice speaks to the “child of reason” and asks where the child has been; the child answers each time with “I have been” or “I saw.” Two readers can take the parts.
evidence: CHILD of reason, whence comest thou?
I have been wandering along the meadows,

questions.prompt: Name the places the child visits and one thing the child noticed in each.
facilitatorNotes: The meadows (cattle, poppies and harebells among the wheat), the forest (whispering wind, a brook, a leaping squirrel) and the night sky (a moon “like a lamp of gold,” stars, then a storm).
evidence: the squirrel leapt from bough to bough;
it was like a lamp of gold.

questions.prompt: Which sentence repeats after each answer, and what does it want the child to notice?
facilitatorNotes: “Return again, child of reason, for there are greater things than these.” It sends the child back to look again and see God in what was seen.
evidence: Return again, child of reason, for there are greater things than these.

questions.prompt: Is the child wrong to describe only what was seen and heard? What does the other voice think is missing?
facilitatorNotes: The child describes carefully and is not wrong; the other voice believes God was in each place and that the child did not perceive it. Some readers think close noticing is already enough; the hymn asks for something more. Discuss both.
evidence: and didst thou not perceive him?
God is in every place;

readings.title: Hymn VII (“Come, let us go into the thick shade”)
readings.challenge: Follow the hymn’s worry and its answers, one after another.
readings.focus: Resting in the shade at noon, the children wonder whether anyone so young can speak to God.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” Noon is the middle of the day; to lisp is to speak like a very small child; to fashion is to shape; nimble means quick and light on one’s feet.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share.

excerpt.locator: Hymn VII, the complete hymn; opens “COME, let us go into the thick shade, for it is the noon of day, and the summer sun beats…”; closes “…we come in; when we sleep, and we wake, his praise shall dwell continually upon our lips.”.

questions.prompt: Where do the speakers go, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Into the thick shade by a brook, because it is noon and the summer sun is hot.
evidence: the summer sun beats hot upon our heads.

questions.prompt: What do the branches do, according to the hymn?
facilitatorNotes: They meet overhead and shut out the sun “as with a green curtain.”
evidence: the branches meet above our heads, and shut out the sun, as with a green curtain;

questions.prompt: The children worry that they are too young and small to speak to God. What answers does the hymn give?
facilitatorNotes: He hears even a whisper; he thought of them before they could think of him; and he taught them to speak, so their lisping praise is fitting. The hymn turns their smallness into a reason to speak.
evidence: for he heareth us when we only whisper;
When we could not think of him, he thought of us;

questions.prompt: The hymn admits, “We cannot be good, as God is good, to all persons every where.” What does it say we can do instead? Is that a satisfying answer?
facilitatorNotes: Rejoice that everywhere there is a God to do people good. Some readers find that comforting; others think we should still try to help people far away. Either view can be argued from the text.
evidence: We cannot be good, as God is good, to all persons every where;
but we can rejoice, that every where there is a God to do them good.

readings.title: Hymn VIII (“See where stands the cottage of the labourer”)
readings.challenge: Follow a picture that keeps growing, from one cottage to the whole world.
readings.focus: Families, villages and kingdoms make up one human family, and the hymn speaks to its weakest and its most powerful.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” Thatch is a roof of straw; to till is to plough; a magistrate is a local judge; a monarch is a king or queen; “mean” here means poor and humble; forlorn means alone and hopeless.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share. The hymn speaks to an enslaved African woman as “Negro woman,” the word of its time; Barbauld opposed the slave trade, and here insists that God sees a woman no one else pities. The hymn also calls the father “the master” of the family, a view of its time.

excerpt.locator: Hymn VIII, the complete hymn; opens “SEE where stands the cottage of the labourer, covered with warm thatch; the mother is…”; closes “…him not worship him: is there any one whom he hath not blessed? let him not praise him.”.

questions.prompt: The hymn begins with one cottage and keeps growing. Put its steps in order.
facilitatorNotes: A family, a village, a town, a kingdom, and then the whole world, which “God governeth.”
evidence: This is a village;
make up this whole world–God governeth it.

questions.prompt: What does a family share, according to the hymn?
facilitatorNotes: One house, one roof, the same bread and the same prayers; they mourn together when one is sick and rejoice together when one is happy.
evidence: they sleep beneath one roof; they eat of the same bread;
If one is sick, they mourn together;

questions.prompt: How does the hymn show that people around the world are different? What does it say they have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Some live in hot sun, some wear furs, and they drink different things and pray in different languages. All are “God’s family,” and he understands every language.
evidence: they pray to him in different languages, but he understandeth them all;
All are God's family;

questions.prompt: The hymn speaks first to a captive woman and then to a powerful monarch. Why might Barbauld put them side by side? What does she tell each one?
facilitatorNotes: They are the weakest and the strongest people imaginable. The woman is told God sees and pities her; the monarch is told God is above him and will punish him if he does wrong. The pairing says that in God’s family no one is too low to be protected or too high to be judged.
evidence: though no one seeth thee, God seeth thee;
boast not thyself as though there were none above thee

readings.title: Hymn IX (“Come, let us walk abroad”)
readings.challenge: Keep track of a long list of plants by where each one grows, then find the questions the hymn keeps asking.
readings.focus: Plants growing everywhere, unplanted and in order, become the hymn’s evidence for a maker.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” To “tell” the grains one by one is to count them; innumerable means too many to count. Mallow, hop, heathflower and laurustinus are plants; the hop climbs a pole with its tendrils. A passenger here is a passer-by; mould is soft earth; verdure is green growth. Enamelleth means coats with bright colour, as enamel coats metal.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share.

excerpt.locator: Hymn IX, the complete hymn; opens “COME, let us walk abroad; let us talk of the works of God.”; closes “…that know the most, will praise God the best; but which of us can number half his works?”.

questions.prompt: The hymn begins with two counting games. What are they, and why can’t anyone win?
facilitatorNotes: Count the grains in a handful of sand, and the blades of grass or the leaves on the trees. They are “innumerable”: too many to count. The hymn then says God’s works are many more.
evidence: number the grains of it;
You cannot count them, they are innumerable;

questions.prompt: Choose three plants from the hymn and say where each one grows.
facilitatorNotes: For example: the fir on the high mountain, the willow above the stream, the daisy under people’s feet, the iris in the marsh, water-lilies under the stream, the wall-flower in hard stone among ruins. The list covers every kind of place.
evidence: The fir groweth on the high mountain,
the wall-flower takes root in the hard stone,

questions.prompt: Who planted the wild flowers, according to the hymn? Where do they grow?
facilitatorNotes: No person did: “The hand of man hath not planted them.” They grow on steep rocks, in bogs, forests and desert islands, everywhere.
evidence: The hand of man hath not planted them;
they spring up every where,

questions.prompt: Find two of the hymn’s “Who…?” or “How…?” questions. What answer does the hymn expect, and how do the questions help it make its argument?
facilitatorNotes: “Who causeth them to grow every where…?” and “How can a small seed contain a plant?” The hymn expects the answer “God,” and says so at the end: “every thing speaks of him.” Asking instead of telling lets children wonder first. Some readers will want to add what scientists now know about seeds and wind; both kinds of answer can be discussed without mocking either.
evidence: How can a small seed contain a plant?
There is little need that I should tell you of God, for every thing speaks of him.

questions.prompt: The hymn says, “Every field is like an open book.” What can a field “say” to someone who looks closely?
facilitatorNotes: The hymn means each flower carries a lesson, and every brook and wind has a voice that speaks of their maker. Readers may name their own lessons from a field: seasons, order, patience. Accept answers that come from looking.
evidence: Every field is like an open book;
Every murmuring brook hath a tongue;

readings.title: Hymns X and XI (“Child of mortality” and its answer)
readings.challenge: Read two hymns as a question and its answer, noticing how the same pattern is turned around.
readings.focus: One hymn weeps because everything dies; the next answers that life returns.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” Hymn X speaks to a weeping child and Hymn XI answers it, so they are read together. Mortality means having to die; a countenance is a face; verdure is green leaves; nipt and lopt are old spellings of nipped and lopped (cut). A pike is a fish. “The spoiler” is death. In Hymn XI the insect that spins “a tomb” is a caterpillar making its cocoon; redeemed means saved.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share. Hymn X is about death: a rose, a tree, insects and a man all die. Hymn XI answers with the Christian belief in resurrection.

excerpt.locator: Hymn X and Hymn XI, both complete hymns; opens “CHILD of mortality, whence comest thou? why is thy countenance sad, and why are thine…”; closes “…of God, is subdued: Jesus hath conquered death:–child of immortality! mourn no longer.”.

questions.prompt: Hymn X tells of four things the speaker saw and then saw again. What were they, and what had happened to each?
facilitatorNotes: A rose (dying on its stalk), a great tree (cut, rotted and fallen), bright insects (eaten or drowned), and a strong man (lying stiff and cold). Each time the pattern is “I have seen … I returned.”
evidence: it spread its leaves to the morning sun–I returned, it was dying upon its stalk;
he lay stiff and cold on the bare ground;

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker of Hymn X weep?
facilitatorNotes: “Because DEATH is in the world”: everything that is born must die. Printing DEATH in capitals makes it sound like a great enemy.
evidence: therefore do I weep, because DEATH is in the world;
all that is born, must die.

questions.prompt: Hymn XI uses the same pattern, “I have seen … I looked again.” What three things come back to life?
facilitatorNotes: The withered flower sprouts new buds; the sun sets and rises again; the caterpillar that lay in its silken “tomb” bursts out with coloured wings. The pattern is turned around: this time the second look brings life.
evidence: I looked again, and it sprung forth afresh;
I looked again, it had burst its tomb;

questions.prompt: Hymn X calls the reader “Child of mortality”; Hymn XI ends with “child of immortality.” What has changed, and why might the author end with those words?
facilitatorNotes: Mortality means having to die; immortality means living for ever. The hymn says that Jesus has conquered death, so the child need not mourn. That is the author’s Christian belief. Readers who see it differently can still notice how one word answers the other.
evidence: CHILD of mortality, whence comest thou?
child of immortality! mourn no longer.

readings.title: Hymn XII (“There is a land”)
readings.challenge: Follow the “but” pattern of the opening, then see how the hymn describes a place with no “but.”
readings.focus: The last hymn describes heaven by taking away everything that spoils good things on earth.
readings.context: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825) was an English poet and teacher. Her Hymns in Prose for Children (1781) were meant to be learned by heart and said aloud; she chose prose instead of rhyme, built each hymn from repeated sentence patterns, and joined the idea of God to things a child can see and hear. Older verb forms such as “taketh” mean “takes,” and “thou” and “thee” mean “you.” This is the last hymn in the book. Myriads are huge numbers; cherubim are angels; hen-bane is a poisonous plant; a desart is a desert. Abraham, Moses, Elijah, Daniel and the shepherd king David (“the son of Jesse”) are people from the Bible. People once believed toads could spit poison; they cannot.
readings.contentNote: This eighteenth-century Christian hymn speaks from its author’s faith; its statements about God are her beliefs, which readers may or may not share. It speaks of parents and friends who have died.

excerpt.locator: Hymn XII, the complete hymn; opens “The rose is sweet, but it is surrounded with thorns: the lily of the valley is fragrant,…”; closes “…to be here but for a little while, and there for ever, even for ages of eternal years.”.

questions.prompt: In the first three sentences, what spoils each good thing? Give two examples.
facilitatorNotes: The rose has thorns; the lily grows among brambles; spring soon passes; winter destroys summer’s beauty; the rainbow vanishes; life is “swallowed up in death.” Each sentence turns on “but.”
evidence: The rose is sweet, but it is surrounded with thorns:
The rainbow is very glorious, but it soon vanisheth away:

questions.prompt: How is “that land” different? Find two things that are there and two that are not.
facilitatorNotes: Roses without thorns, eternal spring, the tree of life, flowers that never fade; no winter cold, no summer scorching, no sickness, no wars or quarrels. It is described by taking the “but” away.
evidence: There is a land, where the roses are without thorns,
In that country there are no wars nor quarrels,

questions.prompt: What does the hymn promise about parents and friends who have died?
facilitatorNotes: That “there we shall embrace them again” and never be separated. Handle gently with children who have lost someone; the hymn speaks from the author’s faith, and families may answer in their own ways.
evidence: When our parents and friends die, and are laid in the cold ground,
and be separated no more.

questions.prompt: The hymn says the earth is “pleasant” but that country is “far better.” Does it want children to love the earth, or to wait for heaven? Use the hymn’s words.
facilitatorNotes: Both: “This earth is pleasant, for it is God’s earth,” yet “That happy land is our home.” Some readers will feel the hymn asks them to enjoy the earth while thinking often of heaven; others may feel it makes earth seem less important. Either is defensible from the last paragraphs.
evidence: This earth is pleasant, for it is God's earth,
That happy land is our home:
